topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; competency frameworks may need adaptation for Australian health systems, workforce structures, and regulatory environment.
takeaways: Map existing digital health competency frameworks to identify gaps in your organisation's current capability assessment tools, rather than building from scratch.
Benchmark your team's AI literacy requirements against established European standards, but validate which competencies are most critical for your specific Australian health service context.
Use the framework's structured approach to competency domains to design targeted upskilling pathways for staff at different levels, from foundational awareness to specialist digital health roles.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely focused on public health education contexts, possibly US-based given Frontiers journal scope. Generalisability to other sectors and geographies unclear without full text, though faculty development principles may have broader application.
takeaways: Design faculty development programmes that move beyond awareness-raising to build genuine competence — resistance often stems from perceived irrelevance or lack of practical skills, so embed AI literacy into existing public health curricula and teaching practices.

Position faculty members as change agents rather than resistors — structured professional development that acknowledges their expertise and concerns is more likely to shift mindsets than top-down mandates.
Create peer-learning and community-of-practice structures where faculty can experiment with AI tools in low-stakes environments before integrating them into teaching and research.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Moderate — addresses Gen Z AI skills development globally, but lacks specific data on geographic scope, sample composition, or sector focus. Findings may be most relevant to educational institutions and policymakers rather than organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify which AI literacy competencies your organisation values most for Gen Z hires, then map gaps between what educational institutions teach and what your roles require — use this to inform graduate recruitment and onboarding strategies.

Consider partnering with educational providers or designing internal micro-credentials that address the specific AI skills gap identified in your sector, rather than assuming Gen Z arrivals are uniformly prepared.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to middle school education context; geographic scope unclear from title and snippet alone. Findings on AI competency frameworks may apply across English-speaking education systems but implementation would need adaptation for different curricula.
takeaways: AI literacy for younger learners should be embedded within broader digital literacy rather than taught in isolation — this integrated approach helps students understand AI's real-world context and limits.

Middle school is a critical intervention point for building foundational AI competencies before students encounter AI tools in higher education and workplaces — early exposure supports later capability development.

A holistic framework approach addresses multiple dimensions (technical understanding, ethical reasoning, critical evaluation) rather than coding skills alone, which is more relevant for non-technical professional roles.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely focuses on higher education contexts globally, but generalisability to workplace AI literacy development in non-academic settings may be limited. Specific applicability to your organisational psychology context requires reviewing the full article's scope.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most relevant to your workforce—technical, analytical, or strategic—and design targeted development pathways rather than generic 'AI for everyone' programs.
Consider whether higher education pedagogical approaches (problem-based learning, project work) could be adapted for employee AI capability building in your organisational context.
Use higher education frameworks as a benchmark to assess gaps in your current AI literacy offerings, particularly around foundational knowledge versus hands-on application.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context; applicability to corporate or vocational settings requires adaptation. The four-domain model may be discipline-specific to academic management.
takeaways: AI literacy functions as a foundational meta-skill that enables learning of other AI-related competencies; assess whether your organisation treats it as a prerequisite capability rather than a standalone module.

The four-domain framework can be used to audit gaps in your workforce's AI readiness across multiple competency areas — map your current training to each domain to identify which areas need strengthening.

Higher education's approach to embedding AI literacy across management roles may offer a template for designing organisational capability-building programs, though implementation will differ in corporate contexts.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — without access to the full article, the generalisability depends on sample size, sector diversity, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. The relationships tested (AI usage → work engagement → creativity) may vary significantly across different organisational contexts and cultures.
takeaways: Employee work engagement appears to be a key mechanism through which AI usage influences creativity — focus on maintaining or enhancing engagement when implementing AI tools, rather than assuming AI tools alone will boost creative output.

Technology acceptance is a critical factor that amplifies or dampens the creativity benefits of AI — invest in change management and user training to build genuine acceptance of AI tools, not just adoption.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings on psychological ownership and AI crafting may be limited to organizational contexts with paternalistic leadership structures, which are more common in certain cultures (e.g., East Asia). Generalisability to Western hierarchical and egalitarian organizational models requires caution.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customizing and adapting AI systems to their workflows—this strengthens collaboration and engagement with AI rather than treating AI as an imposed external tool.

In paternalistic leadership environments, leverage leaders' mentoring relationships to encourage 'AI crafting' (active modification and personalization of AI)—this bridges the gap between top-down AI adoption and genuine employee buy-in.

Design onboarding and training programs that position employees as active shapers of AI implementation, not passive users—psychological ownership of the AI integration process itself predicts better collaboration outcomes than compliance-focused approaches.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The moderating effects of self-efficacy and transformational leadership may vary across industries, organisational cultures, and geographic contexts. Results likely applicable across sectors experiencing AI implementation.
takeaways: Leaders can mitigate AI-related job insecurity by demonstrating transformational leadership behaviours — emphasise vision, provide individualised support, and model confidence in employees' capacity to adapt to AI tools.

Invest in building employee self-efficacy around AI use through targeted training and skill-building programs; employees with higher self-efficacy experience less job insecurity when AI is introduced.

Combine leadership interventions with capability development — neither transformational leadership nor self-efficacy alone fully buffers job insecurity; both are needed for effective change management during AI adoption.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — generalisability depends on sample size, sector focus (cybersecurity), and geographic scope, which are not provided in the snippet. Findings may be limited to cybersecurity professionals or specific organisational contexts.
takeaways: AI self-efficacy acts as a protective mechanism that buffers the negative effects of job stress on cybersecurity compliance behaviour — consider screening and upskilling staff in AI literacy to reduce stress-related lapses in security practices.

Job stress mediates the relationship between uncertainty and cybersecurity outcomes — workload and role clarity interventions may be as important as technical security training for improving behavioural compliance.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — likely limited by unstated sample characteristics, geography, and sector specificity. Full methodology needed to assess applicability to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Employees' psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) appears to be a key driver of how they leverage AI tools as job resources rather than threats — consider assessing and developing these dimensions when implementing AI systems.

In algorithm-driven roles, building psychological capital may be more impactful than technical training alone for fostering innovation and adaptive use of AI — identify staff with lower resilience or efficacy and provide targeted support during AI adoption.

Frame AI implementation conversations around employee agency and growth potential rather than automation risk — this psychological framing may unlock greater innovation and engagement with algorithmic tools.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects APA perspective on US workforce trends. While uncertainty about AI adoption is global, specific labour market conditions, employment protections, and psychological support infrastructure differ significantly between the US and Australia.
takeaways: Acknowledge that AI-driven workplace uncertainty is a legitimate source of employee stress and anxiety; proactive psychological safety messaging can help reduce rumination and catastrophising about job security.

Consider offering employee assistance programs (EAPs) or mental health support specifically addressing AI transition concerns, rather than assuming employees will self-manage anxiety about technological change.

Create transparent communication channels about organisational AI adoption timelines and skill development pathways — ambiguity and lack of information tend to amplify psychological distress during technological transitions.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner report based on consulting experience, likely skewed toward large organisations with resources for formal change programmes. Geographic scope unclear; may reflect primarily US/Western consulting contexts.
takeaways: Shift from 'AI adoption' framing to 'AI adaptation' — reframe change initiatives around building new human behaviours and ways of working, not just tool implementation.

Design change programmes to target specific behaviours needed for AI success (e.g. collaborative problem-solving, comfort with ambiguity, continuous learning) rather than assuming technical training alone drives capability.
Use structured change methodology to support behavioural shifts, not just communication campaigns — this likely includes assessment, feedback, reinforcement, and peer modelling.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or sample. Insights may reflect US business school priorities and may not generalise to other sectors, geographies, or organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation that AI could augment rather than replace, and pilot changes with clear success metrics before full rollout to build employee buy-in.

Design upskilling programmes that help employees understand which capabilities remain uniquely human (e.g. judgment, relationship-building, creativity) so they see their role evolving rather than becoming obsolete.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study sample details not provided in snippet. The approach-avoidance framework is theoretically applicable across organisational contexts, but geographic scope and sector representation are unclear.
takeaways: Use an approach-avoidance lens when designing AI adoption programs — some employees may proactively reshape their roles (approach) while others withdraw or minimise AI-related tasks (avoidance), requiring differentiated support strategies.

Monitor job crafting behaviors during AI rollout as an early indicator of engagement levels; employees who avoid AI-related job redesign may be experiencing anxiety or skills gaps that warrant targeted intervention.
Design change communications that highlight opportunities for role enhancement rather than task displacement to encourage approach-oriented job crafting and reduce avoidance responses to AI adoption.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG perspective based on consulting experience across clients, but specific organisational contexts, industries, and geographies not detailed in snippet. Findings likely most applicable to large enterprises undertaking AI transformation.
takeaways: Position AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation—design change management and learning programmes around shifting roles and skills, not just tool rollout.
Embed workforce planning into AI strategy from the outset: identify which capabilities need development, which roles will change, and which teams need upskilling before deployment begins.

Use AI transformation as a catalyst for behaviour change by reframing it as career development and organisational renewal, rather than a threat—this improves engagement and adoption rates across the workforce.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors and geographies, but lacks peer-reviewed empirical validation and may reflect practices skewed toward large enterprises.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as organisational change management rather than purely technical training — this shifts focus from individual skill acquisition to systemic adoption readiness and cultural transformation.

Treat AI capability development as a strategic priority requiring executive sponsorship and integrated change communications, not as a siloed L&D initiative, to increase uptake and sustained behaviour change.

Identify and address resistance and readiness barriers early through stakeholder engagement and feedback loops, rather than assuming training alone will drive adoption of new AI-enabled ways of working.

articles.title: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. Conservation of Resources theory provides a solid theoretical framework, but findings may be limited by sector, organisational context, and geographic scope of the study population.
takeaways: Employee attitudes toward AI (liking/comfort) act as a critical moderator of adoption outcomes — organisations should assess and actively work to improve AI acceptance before rolling out new tools, rather than assuming adoption alone drives positive outcomes.

Job crafting and career commitment may be mechanisms through which AI adoption affects employee wellbeing — design implementation strategies that help employees reshape their roles proactively and reinforce career development opportunities when introducing generative AI.

Use a Conservation of Resources lens when planning AI change initiatives: employees experiencing resource depletion may struggle more with adoption, so consider workload, support systems, and skill development as foundational before expecting positive employee outcomes.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Findings depend on sample characteristics not detailed in snippet; generalisability cannot be fully assessed without access to methodology.
takeaways: Some people's brains are wired to remember shocking or unexpected moments better than others—and your personality type influences which surprises stick with you.
Introverts and extroverts may encode surprising events differently in memory, suggesting that how 'shocking' something feels is partly baked into who we are rather than purely situational.

Your personality doesn't just shape how you behave in the moment—it actually changes what your brain decides is worth remembering, which is a neat illustration of how deeply personality reaches into cognition.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on wine review text analysis; findings may not generalise beyond wine appreciation or to non-English speaking populations.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from seemingly mundane consumer choices like wine preferences, suggesting our everyday tastes reveal more about who we are than we might realise.
Wine reviews — often written casually and without self-consciousness — turned out to be a goldmine for personality prediction, showing that unguarded language choices are surprisingly revealing.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven news report without access to the underlying research methodology, sample size, or institutional context. Actual generalisability depends on the original study details not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Brain imaging is revealing structural or functional differences in psychopathic individuals that may help explain differences in emotional processing or decision-making — a reminder that personality traits we think of as purely behavioural often have measurable neural signatures.
The framing of psychopathy as 'shocking' highlights how neuroscience findings can challenge everyday intuitions about human nature, even when the specific difference is routine in scientific terms.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — twin study methodology suggests likely Western sample, but geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that authoritarian political beliefs have a surprisingly heritable component — meaning your genes influence your politics more than we might intuitively expect, not just your upbringing or environment.

The finding challenges the assumption that political ideology is purely a product of conscious reasoning or life experience, suggesting innate personality traits and predispositions play a measurable role.

This research highlights how nature and nurture interact in shaping something we often think of as entirely chosen — our political worldview — making it a fascinating window into what we inherit versus what we develop.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — Cambridge research on music and personality typically uses large, cross-cultural datasets, though specific methodology cannot be confirmed from the snippet alone.
takeaways: People's taste in music reveals consistent personality patterns worldwide, suggesting that what we listen to reflects something fundamental about how we're wired rather than just cultural conditioning.

The finding flips the assumption that music preference is purely cultural — instead, personality traits appear to drive musical choices in remarkably similar ways across different countries and populations.
It's a surprisingly tidy result: the music someone loves can tell you something reliable about their personality no matter where they're from, which is oddly reassuring in our fragmented world.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear — snippet provides insufficient detail on study location, sample size, or methodology to assess generalisability. The underlying research may be limited in scope.
takeaways: A medical condition affecting metabolism (hyperthyroidism) correlates with personality traits associated with narcissism, psychopathy, or similar characteristics — a counterintuitive link between endocrine function and psychological traits.

The finding suggests physical health conditions can have unexpected connections to how we think and behave, raising questions about whether personality variations might sometimes have biological roots we haven't considered.

It's the kind of surprising connection that makes you wonder what other hidden relationships exist between our bodies and our behaviour — and why this particular link hasn't been more widely noticed before.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on academic team contexts; generalisability to non-academic organisational settings and beyond multicultural academic teams unclear without access to full methodology.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to support inclusive leadership practices, particularly around gender equity in diverse teams — consider how your organisation might pilot AI-assisted feedback or decision-support systems that flag unconscious bias in team dynamics.

Inclusive leadership in multicultural settings requires attention to both gender and cultural dimensions; AI-assisted approaches may help standardise fairness in how these intersecting identities are valued and included in team processes.

Psychological safety depends partly on whether team members perceive leadership as genuinely inclusive — ensure any AI system supporting inclusive leadership is transparent about its role and limitations to maintain trust.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad — PwC surveys typically reach thousands of workers across multiple countries and sectors, though specific sample composition and methodology are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Identify which workforce concerns (hopes vs. fears) are most prevalent in your organisation by comparing internal survey data against PwC's global benchmarks — this reveals whether psychological safety issues are sector-wide or organisation-specific.

Use the survey findings to shape leadership conversations about worker anxieties (e.g., job security, AI impact, work environment) and design targeted interventions to address the top concerns affecting psychological safety in your context.
Monitor how hope and fear ratios shift year-on-year to assess whether your organisation's culture-building or change management efforts are improving employee confidence and willingness to speak up.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — sample size and geographic scope not evident from title and snippet. Findings on AI adoption's link to employee depression via psychological safety require verification across different organisational contexts and geographies.
takeaways: Monitor psychological safety closely during AI implementation; low psychological safety may amplify employee anxiety and depression risk when introducing AI tools.
Ethical leadership is a critical moderator during AI adoption — leaders who transparently communicate AI's purpose, manage fears, and involve employees in implementation can protect mental wellbeing.
Screen for depression risk factors in teams undergoing rapid AI adoption, particularly among employees with lower baseline psychological safety or trust in management.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report likely draws on case studies or client work rather than systematic research; geographic scope and sector details unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Psychological safety can help address inequality and create more equitable participation across diverse employee groups — consider auditing team dynamics to identify whose voices are being heard and create explicit norms that welcome contribution from quieter members.

When designing psychological safety interventions, frame the business case around levelling the playing field and reducing barriers to contribution, not just improving morale — this resonates with equity commitments and talent retention.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on observations and expert commentary without empirical data. Likely reflects dynamics in knowledge-work sectors but generalisability to other industries or geographies unclear.
takeaways: Lack of clear AI policies and fear of misuse creates a trust deficit — establish explicit, non-punitive guidelines about acceptable AI use to encourage employees to disclose rather than hide their practices.
Psychological safety around AI adoption requires leaders to model transparency about their own AI usage and create channels for questions without fear of judgment or disciplinary action.

Address the root cause of non-disclosure by communicating how AI usage data will be used; employees are more likely to be transparent if they understand the purpose isn't surveillance but capability building.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM content is US-focused and reflects US HR practices and employment law. The psychological safety principles may be applicable more broadly, but specific implementation guidance is tailored to US organisational contexts.
takeaways: Leaders should create explicit norms where team members feel safe admitting mistakes and asking questions without fear of embarrassment or retaliation — this requires modelling vulnerability and responding constructively to errors.

Practical actions include soliciting input from quieter team members, responding non-defensively to criticism, and following through on commitments — these behaviours signal trustworthiness and reduce perceived interpersonal risk in teams.
